Start with the youngest passengers. Any child younger than eight riding in a vehicle in Arizona has to be properly secured in a child passenger restraint system. Then we look at head restraints and how to set them, and finally the exhaust rules for mufflers, emissions systems and fumes. Each of these items protects someone, either the people in the car or the people and air around it, so learn what each rule requires. The child restraint rule covers every child younger than eight, whatever kind of trip it is.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Head restraints","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"They reduce whiplash risk.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]},{"text":"Set against the back of the head.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]},{"text":"Level with the middle of the ear.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is what a head restraint is for. Head restraints on seat backs exist to lower the risk of a whiplash injury when you are hit from behind. Its position matters. An adjustable head restraint should sit against the back of your head, level with the middle of your ear. Set that way, it can do the job the manual describes: lowering the risk of whiplash when you are hit from behind. The two facts work together: the purpose is to lower whiplash risk in a rear-end hit, and the position, against the back of the head at the middle of the ear, is what makes that possible.","fact_ids":["sec05-F02","sec05-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s3","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Not the top of the head","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Middle of the ear.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F03"]},{"text":"Touching the back of the head.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F03"]},{"text":"Not low at the neck.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a mistake many drivers make. They push the head restraint all the way up or leave it at its lowest setting. The manual is precise about the right spot. A head restraint lines up with the middle of the ear and touches the back of the head; it is not set to the top of the head or left low at the neck. So the target is the middle of your ear, with the restraint against the back of your head. Anything higher or lower misses the mark the manual sets. The same position, level with the middle of the ear, applies to every adjustable head restraint.","fact_ids":["sec05-R04","sec05-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Mufflers","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Working at all times.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"No excessive pollution or noise.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},{"text":"Cut-outs and bypasses are illegal.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Every vehicle's exhaust starts with the muffler. Every motor vehicle needs a muffler that works well and runs at all times, so it does not cause excessive pollution or unusual noise. The manual also bans ways around it. Fitting a muffler cut-out, a bypass or any similar device is illegal. So the muffler must stay in place and working, and anything that lets exhaust skip it is against the law. So two rules apply to the muffler at once: it must be working and running at all times, and nothing may be fitted to let the exhaust bypass it.","fact_ids":["sec05-F04","sec05-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Emissions and fumes","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Emissions system on newer models.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R03"]},{"text":"No excessive fumes or smoke.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R03"]},{"text":"Different from the muffler rule.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Motor vehicles of the nineteen sixty-seven model year or newer must have an exhaust emissions system to help cut air pollution. The engine rule covers every vehicle. The engine of every motor vehicle must be equipped so that excessive fumes and smoke cannot escape. The manual separates the muffler rule from the emissions rule: the muffler rule targets noise and pollution and bans bypass devices, while the emissions rule requires an exhaust emissions system on nineteen sixty-seven and newer models. Each rule covers a different part of the exhaust.","fact_ids":["sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the head restraint","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-R04","sec05-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Adjusting the head restraint.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-R04","sec05-F02"]},{"text":"Where should it sit?","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-R04","sec05-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: where should an adjustable head restraint be set? The answer is against the back of your head, level with the middle of your ear. An adjustable head restraint should sit against the back of your head, level with the middle of your ear. If you said the top of the head, look again at the manual's correction. A head restraint lines up with the middle of the ear and touches the back of the head; it is not set to the top of the head or left low at the neck. The right setting is what lets the restraint lower your whiplash risk.","fact_ids":["sec05-F03","sec05-R04","sec05-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Equipment recap","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Children under eight restrained.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Head restraint at mid ear.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},{"text":"Working muffler, emissions system, no smoke.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close, any child younger than eight riding in Arizona must be properly secured in a child passenger restraint system. Head restraints lower whiplash risk and should sit against the back of your head, level with the middle of your ear. Every vehicle needs a muffler that works at all times, and cut-outs and bypasses are illegal. Vehicles from the nineteen sixty-seven model year on need an exhaust emissions system, and every engine must keep excessive fumes and smoke from escaping. Each item helps protect the people in the car or the air around it.","fact_ids":["sec05-F01","sec05-F02","sec05-F03","sec05-F04","sec05-F05","sec05-F06","sec05-F07","sec05-R03","sec05-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec05-u02","module_id":"sec05-m02","objective_ids":["sec05-u02"],"title":{"text":"Glass, mirrors, horn and lights","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-R05"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Seeing clearly and being seen and heard are basic to safety, so Arizona sets rules for glass, mirrors, the horn and lights.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F10","sec05-F11"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Raj's pickup is loaded so high that he cannot see out the back window.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Because the load blocks his rear view, he needs a driver-side outside mirror showing at least two hundred feet behind.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-R01"]},"result":{"text":"His horn must also be audible at two hundred feet, the same distance as the mirror rule.","fact_ids":["sec05-F11","sec05-R01"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a broken-down car may use flashing red lights on its front.","fact_ids":["sec05-R02"]},"correction":{"text":"Forward flashing red lights are off-limits to ordinary vehicles even when disabled; use hazard flashers when stopped on the roadway or shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec05-R02","sec05-F13","sec05-F14"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Two hundred to see, two hundred to hear.","fact_ids":["sec05-R01"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Your car is stopped on the shoulder. Which lights should be on?","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02"]},"answer":{"text":"Hazard warning lights.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14"]},"rationale":{"text":"Hazard lights go on whenever you are stopped on the roadway or shoulder, while forward flashing red lights stay banned.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Seeing and being seen","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Windshield and wipers.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Tint, mirrors and horn.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},{"text":"Sirens and lights.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the equipment that helps you see and helps others see and hear you. Start with the glass in front of you. A vehicle must have a windshield with no cracks, and its windshield wipers must work properly. Then we will look at window tint, the outside mirror rule, the horn, who may carry a siren, the ban on forward flashing red lights, and when to use your hazard warning lights. Two of these rules share one distance, which is worth remembering. Each rule is short, but each one is a firm requirement for the vehicle you drive.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Window tint","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Legal within limits only.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Owner should confirm compliance.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"No numbers given in the manual.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Window tint has its own rule. Tint film on windows and windshields is legal only within certain limits, so owners should confirm the maker or installer follows Arizona law. The manual adds a point about what it does and does not say. The manual gives no tint numbers; it says only that tint is lawful within limits and puts the burden on the owner to check that the installer complied. So if you buy a car with tint or have tint installed, the job of confirming it follows Arizona law falls on you as the owner. No tint percentage is given.","fact_ids":["sec05-F09","sec05-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Mirror and horn","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Blocked view: driver-side mirror.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-R01"]},{"text":"Mirror shows two hundred feet behind.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-R01"]},{"text":"Horn heard at two hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here are two equipment rules with numbers. If a vehicle's build or load blocks the driver's rear view, it needs at least one outside mirror on the driver side showing at least two hundred feet of highway behind. Your vehicle must have a working horn that can be heard from two hundred feet away. The manual points out what these two rules have in common. The required outside mirror must show two hundred feet of road behind, and the required horn must be audible at two hundred feet, so one distance covers both rules. One distance, two rules.","fact_ids":["sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Sirens and red lights","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Sirens for emergency vehicles.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},{"text":"No forward flashing red lights.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},{"text":"Exceptions: emergency, school bus, snow removal.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Some equipment is reserved. Emergency vehicles are the ones that may carry a siren, whistle or bell. Lights have a similar rule. Flashing red lights on the front of a vehicle are banned, even on a disabled vehicle, except on authorized emergency vehicles, school buses and snow removal equipment. So an ordinary car may not carry a siren and may not show flashing red lights on its front, whatever its situation. The three exceptions to the red light ban are authorized emergency vehicles, school buses and snow removal equipment, and a disabled ordinary car is not one of them.","fact_ids":["sec05-F12","sec05-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Hazard lights, not red lights","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stopped on road or shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02"]},{"text":"Turn on hazard lights.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02"]},{"text":"Forward red lights stay banned.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. When a car breaks down, a driver may think any flashing light is allowed. The manual draws a clear line. Turn on your hazard warning lights whenever your vehicle is stopped on the roadway or on the shoulder. Hazard flashers are switched on when you are stopped on the roadway or shoulder, while flashing red lights facing forward are off-limits to ordinary vehicles even when they break down. So when you are stopped on the roadway or shoulder, switch on the hazard lights, and leave forward flashing red lights to emergency vehicles, school buses and snow removal equipment.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the lights rule","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02","sec05-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stopped on the shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02","sec05-F13"]},{"text":"Which lights go on?","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02","sec05-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: your car is stopped on the shoulder of the road. Which lights should you turn on? The answer is your hazard warning lights. Turn on your hazard warning lights whenever your vehicle is stopped on the roadway or on the shoulder. Flashing red lights on the front would not be allowed, even though the car is disabled, because those are reserved for emergency vehicles, school buses and snow removal equipment. Hazard flashers are switched on when you are stopped on the roadway or shoulder, while flashing red lights facing forward are off-limits to ordinary vehicles even when they break down.","fact_ids":["sec05-F14","sec05-R02","sec05-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Glass and lights recap","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-F12","sec05-F13","sec05-F14","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Uncracked windshield, working wipers.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-F12","sec05-F13","sec05-F14","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Two hundred feet for mirror and horn.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-F12","sec05-F13","sec05-F14","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R05"]},{"text":"Hazard lights when stopped.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-F12","sec05-F13","sec05-F14","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"To sum up, your windshield must have no cracks and your wipers must work. Window tint is legal only within limits, and the owner should confirm it follows Arizona law. When the vehicle's build or load blocks the rear view, a driver-side outside mirror must show at least two hundred feet behind, and the horn must be audible at two hundred feet. Sirens, whistles and bells are for emergency vehicles, forward flashing red lights are banned on ordinary vehicles, and hazard lights go on whenever you are stopped on the roadway or shoulder.","fact_ids":["sec05-F08","sec05-F09","sec05-F10","sec05-F11","sec05-F12","sec05-F13","sec05-F14","sec05-R01","sec05-R02","sec05-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec05-u03","module_id":"sec05-m03","objective_ids":["sec05-u03"],"title":{"text":"Defensive highest.","fact_ids":["sec05-R06"]},"correction":{"text":"Courtesy and consideration are ranked as the most important attitudes, while concentration and alertness are other important planning.","fact_ids":["sec05-F15","sec05-F16"]},{"text":"Anticipate and act in time.","fact_ids":["sec05-F15","sec05-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about the mindset behind safe driving. Here is how the manual frames it. Driving defensively protects both your life and your driving record, and it starts with constant awareness of conditions and planning ahead. Defensive driving also means anticipating dangers and acting in time so that you never strike an obstacle or another vehicle. In the rest of this lesson we look at what even a small crash can cost, the attitudes the manual ranks highest, the risks of driving tired or upset, and what foresight means.","fact_ids":["sec05-F15","sec05-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What crashes cost","fact_ids":["sec05-F17","sec05-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Inconvenience and repair bills.","fact_ids":["sec05-F17","sec05-F16"]},{"text":"Possible court and fines.","fact_ids":["sec05-F17","sec05-F16"]},{"text":"Higher insurance rates.","fact_ids":["sec05-F17","sec05-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Defensive driving matters even when nobody gets hurt. Even a crash with no injuries brings inconvenience and repair bills, and it can lead to a court appearance, fines and higher insurance rates. Those costs are the reason the manual stresses acting before trouble arrives. Even a minor crash can lead to court, a fine and a higher insurance bill. Put another way, the costs of a crash do not depend on injuries: inconvenience, repair bills, a possible court appearance, fines and higher insurance rates can all follow a crash in which nobody is hurt.","fact_ids":["sec05-F17","sec05-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The key attitudes","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F19"]},"lines":[{"text":"Courtesy and consideration first.","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F19"]},{"text":"Concentration and alertness.","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F19"]},{"text":"Mind on the road.","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F19"]}],"narration":{"text":"The manual ranks attitudes. The manual names courtesy and consideration for others as the most important driving attitudes and the key to safe driving. Then it adds two more. Concentration and alertness also matter, so make keeping your mind on the road a habit. Courtesy shapes how you treat other drivers, and concentration keeps your attention where it belongs. Together these habits describe how a defensive driver thinks: treating others with courtesy and consideration, staying alert, and keeping concentration on the road instead of letting it wander. The manual treats courtesy and consideration as the key to safe driving.","fact_ids":["sec05-F18","sec05-F19"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Which attitude ranks first?","fact_ids":["sec05-R06","sec05-F18","sec05-F19"]},"lines":[{"text":"Courtesy and consideration: most important.","fact_ids":["sec05-R06","sec05-F18","sec05-F19"]},{"text":"Concentration and alertness: also important.","fact_ids":["sec05-R06","sec05-F18","sec05-F19"]},{"text":"Know the order.","fact_ids":["sec05-R06","sec05-F18","sec05-F19"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Because driving takes so much focus, people guess that concentration is the top attitude. The manual says otherwise. Courtesy and consideration are ranked as the most important attitudes, while concentration and alertness are described as other important elements. So when a question asks for the most important attitudes, the answer is courtesy and consideration for others, and concentration and alertness come in as other important elements. Both pairs matter, but the ranking itself is part of what the manual teaches here.","fact_ids":["sec05-R06","sec05-F18","sec05-F19"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":34,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Tired, upset and foresight","fact_ids":["sec05-F20","sec05-F21","sec05-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Drowsy or upset can equal impaired risk.","fact_ids":["sec05-F20","sec05-F21","sec05-R07"]},{"text":"Foresight: size up, be ready.","fact_ids":["sec05-F20","sec05-F21","sec05-R07"]},{"text":"Part of defensive driving.","fact_ids":["sec05-F20","sec05-F21","sec05-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Your own condition affects your safety. Driving while drowsy or emotionally upset can be as dangerous as driving impaired. Defensive driving also needs a particular skill. Foresight is the ability to size up a traffic situation quickly and be ready to take corrective action. The manual explains how that skill fits into the bigger picture. Foresight is about sizing up a situation fast and being ready to correct, while defensive driving is the wider practice of awareness, planning, anticipation and right action. Each idea supports the others.","fact_ids":["sec05-F20","sec05-F21","sec05-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec05-u03-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Everyone meets hazards","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F18","sec05-F20","sec05-F21"]},"lines":[{"text":"Equipment failures and bad weather.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F18","sec05-F20","sec05-F21"]},{"text":"Unskilled and careless drivers.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F18","sec05-F20","sec05-F21"]},{"text":"Defensive driving is the best preparation.","fact_ids":["sec05-F22","sec05-F18","sec05-F20","sec05-F21"]}],"narration":{"text":"No amount of experience removes risk. However many years you have driven, you will eventually meet equipment failures, bad weather, unskilled drivers and drivers who ignore the rules, and defensive driving is the best preparation.
